sections.title: Geopolitics – Key Flashpoints

subsections.text: US-China relations remain in a managed but fragile détente following the September 2026 Trump-Xi Washington summit (the second leaders’ meeting of the year after Beijing in May). The sides extended the October 2025 Busan trade truce by two months to 10 January 2027, agreed reciprocal tariff relief frameworks on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods each way, launched Boards of Trade and Investment plus an AI (“super intelligence”) dialogue, and scheduled further meetings at APEC in Shenzhen (18–19 November) and the G20 in Miami (December). Core differences on Taiwan, advanced technology/export controls, rare earths implementation, and strategic competition persist; a close Trump aide noted that pre-summit issues remain unresolved. The November midterms, in which Democrats captured both the House and Senate in a broad rebuke of Trump (driven by inflation and the Iran conflict), have introduced uncertainty over US delivery capacity and potential congressional pressure on Taiwan arms and tech restrictions. Ukraine-Russia fighting continues at high intensity into day ~1,718 of the full-scale war. Russian strikes have damaged every Ukrainian power plant according to President Zelensky; recent barrages used large numbers of drones and ballistic missiles (including reported North Korean systems), causing blackouts and civilian casualties. Ukrainian long-range strikes hit Russian oil infrastructure. US-brokered talks involving Russia and Ukraine are scheduled for Abu Dhabi (next round ~11 November); territorial and security issues remain far apart. Localized humanitarian pauses (e.g., Oleshky) have occurred but no broader ceasefire holds. In the Middle East, the US-Iran conflict continues with the Strait of Hormuz effectively disrupted for normal commercial traffic since late February 2026. Recent limited US strikes targeted Iranian air defenses (including on Qeshm Island); Iran has used mines, UUVs, and other means against shipping. Houthi forces, with reported Iranian direction and advisors, have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast (seizing Mocha) and intensified ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi infrastructure (airports, Aramco sites, pumping stations). Saudi defenses intercept many but not all threats. Diplomacy via Qatar/Oman and regional actors (including Mecca Pact countries) continues but remains stalled on sequencing of Hormuz reopening versus US blockade relief; Trump has indicated no rush for a deal. Risks of escalation remain elevated.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The US-China trade truce originally set to expire 10 November 2026 was extended through 10 January 2027. This preserves the Busan framework (lowered US tariffs, Chinese rare-earth licensing and agricultural purchase commitments). The Board of Trade has advanced recommendations for reciprocal tariff reductions on ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods each direction (consumer goods, agricultural items, etc.). China has reaffirmed some commitments; the US has pressed for immediate compliance on Busan terms ahead of the Shenzhen APEC meeting. Formal legal notices finalizing all extensions are still pending in places, creating residual uncertainty for importers. Broader structural issues (tech controls, critical minerals processing dominance) are unaddressed. No major new tariff escalations reported in the past week.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen remains under pressure (USD/JPY trading in the high-158 to ~159 area in recent sessions). The Bank of Japan holds its short-term policy rate at 1.25% (hiked in September; held in late October with one dissent). Japan conducted large-scale yen-buying interventions in 2026, including a record ~¥15.4 trillion period in late July–August and earlier spring actions totaling over ¥27 trillion for the year to date; a July 31 coordinated operation with the US Treasury marked the first joint yen-buying in decades. Verbal warnings continue and the 160 level is widely viewed as a soft intervention threshold. Broader central-bank trends show a mild hiking bias: Fed funds at 3.75–4.00%, ECB deposit rate at 2.50%, BoE recently at 4.00%. Rate differentials and energy-driven terms-of-trade shocks continue to favor the dollar versus the yen and euro.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent crude settled near $98/bbl and WTI near $90–91 in early November, well above pre-conflict levels (~$72 Brent) but off peaks above $120. Prices have been highly volatile: a sharp post-midterm sell-off on hopes of de-escalation with Iran, followed by rebounds on continued tanker attacks and limited US strikes. Key drivers are Hormuz traffic constraints (flows far below pre-war ~20+ mb/d averages), Houthi actions, and Saudi infrastructure risks. Gas (TTF, JKM) remains elevated. Short-term outlook is two-sided: further escalation or full Hormuz closure would push prices sharply higher; credible progress toward reopening and Iranian export recovery would unwind the risk premium toward the $70s–80s range. Physical bottlenecks and shipping reroutes persist.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: US headline CPI was 3.7% y/y in September 2026 with core at 2.6%; energy is the primary upward driver. October nonfarm payrolls rose a stronger-than-expected 165k and unemployment fell to 4.1%. The Fed holds the funds rate at 3.75–4.00% (last hike September; held October). The ECB deposit rate is 2.50% (held October after earlier hikes; December hike priced); BOJ at 1.25% with December hike odds elevated. Inflation remains above targets across major economies, supporting a higher-for-longer bias even as growth holds up. Bond markets continue to reflect term-premium and fiscal concerns alongside energy-driven inflation risks.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler and semiconductor capital expenditure remains on a multi-hundred-billion to ~$1 trillion annual trajectory, driven by data-center build-out for training and inference. Tightest physical bottlenecks include gas turbines and grid interconnections (multi-year lead times), transformers/switchgear, rare-earth magnets (China dominates mining/processing), leading-edge logic (TSMC concentration), advanced packaging, HBM/DRAM, and optical components. Power availability is already delaying deployments. Capital markets show early signs of strain (funding rounds scaled back; credit concerns). Geopolitical exposure is acute: US-China tensions, export controls, and Chinese leverage over critical minerals create single-point failure risks for the entire stack. Diversification efforts are underway but years from scale.

subsections.text: U.S.-China relations remain focused on managed stability ahead of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen (18–19 November). Presidents Trump and Xi met twice earlier in 2026 (Beijing in May, Washington state visit 23–25 September). The September summit produced a two-month extension of the Busan/Kuala Lumpur trade truce to 10 January 2027, reciprocal tariff reductions on ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, establishment of U.S.-China Boards of Trade and Investment, an agricultural working group, an AI (“super intelligence”) dialogue, fentanyl-related measures, and continued high-level dialogue mechanisms. China has confirmed discussions on a possible Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral on the APEC sidelines; Beijing is interested in the optics while substantive outcomes remain uncertain. Post-U.S. midterm results (Democratic gains in Congress) have led analysts to note short-term Chinese leverage in talks but longer-term risks from a more constrained Trump or a less accommodating successor, including pressure on Taiwan arms sales. The U.S.-Iran conflict (ongoing into its ninth month, Day ~252 as of early November) continues with shipping attacks and mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz, IRGC claims of downing U.S. drones, and Trump stating an imminent decision on further strikes or a deal. Saudi-Houthi fighting has escalated, with Houthi ballistic missile and drone claims against Saudi airports (Riyadh, Dammam, Medina area) and Saudi interceptions/strikes in Yemen; Houthis have advanced in parts of Lahij and seek recognition of control. Iranian officials have engaged Russia (and previously China) on negotiations. Oil markets have reacted sharply to midterm outcomes and Hormuz risks. Ukraine-Russia fighting persists with mutual long-range strikes. Zelenskyy stated that every Ukrainian power plant has been damaged; Russia continues energy infrastructure attacks causing regional outages. Ukraine has struck Russian oil refineries (e.g., Ryazan). Limited humanitarian progress includes the Oleshky ceasefire. U.S. envoys (Kushner, Witkoff) held productive talks in Brussels on security guarantees and reconstruction; further U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks are expected in Abu Dhabi. Trump has described the war as close to settlement involving Europe; Russia continues to reject broad ceasefires while using humanitarian issues for leverage. Front-line advances remain limited and costly.

sections.title: Geopolitics – Key Flashpoints

subsections.text: U.S.-China relations remain in a managed detente following the September 2026 Washington summit, where Presidents Trump and Xi reaffirmed a framework of “constructive strategic stability” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. A two-month extension of the October 2025 Busan trade truce (to January 10, 2027) was confirmed, alongside operationalization of Boards of Trade and Investment, a reciprocal ~$30 billion non-sensitive goods tariff-reduction framework, Chinese coal import commitments, and establishment of a U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue (next exchange targeted for November). Differences persist on rare earths/critical minerals, Taiwan (including prior large U.S. arms packages), advanced semiconductors/export controls, and fentanyl. Further leader meetings are scheduled at APEC in Shenzhen (November) and the G20 in Miami (December). Underlying competition continues, with Beijing emphasizing managed rivalry over confrontation. The U.S.-Iran conflict (ongoing since early 2026; ~Day 246 as of October 31) centers on the Strait of Hormuz, tanker incidents (including mines), and Iranian threats of broader retaliation. Trump has stated the war will “get wrapped up soon,” while Qatari (and Mecca Pact: Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey) mediators continue indirect talks on sequencing concessions such as Hormuz reopening versus U.S. naval restrictions. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has directed preparations for expanded targeting if strikes resume. U.S. officials have signaled readiness for potential post-midterm (November 3) military options, with force posture (including carrier/amphibious deployments) reinforced; no final decision is reported, and pre-election strikes have been ruled out. Houthi activity remains elevated against Saudi infrastructure, airports (including Aden), and the Yemeni government-aligned forces, with Saudi intercepts and ground fighting around Taiz-Aden routes continuing. Israel’s recent election produced no clear majority. In Ukraine, a localized humanitarian ceasefire in occupied Oleshky (Kherson) has held longer than prior truces, enabling demining and civilian evacuations/aid. Broader fighting continues: Russian drone/missile strikes (including a Dnipro rail platform attack killing 14) and Ukrainian long-range hits on Russian defense industry and oil refining (Rostov, Ufa). Russian casualties are reported at elevated monthly levels. The Kremlin rejects a large-scale frontline ceasefire. U.S. approval of a substantial PAC-3 Patriot package for Ukraine was announced (delivery timeline multi-year). Diplomatic activity includes G20 foreign ministers’ meetings and limited trilateral contacts. Other notes: North Korean missile testing and South China Sea friction persist at low intensity.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China truce is intact through January 10, 2027. Implementation includes the two-month port-fee/shipping pause extension (USTR proposal process underway), suspension of certain Chinese rare-earth export controls and U.S. BIS Affiliates Rule expansion, and progress on the $30 billion reciprocal non-sensitive goods framework (U.S. exports: agriculture, seafood, wood, cosmetics, medical devices; Chinese: appliances, toys, holiday goods, car seats). Agricultural purchases and critical-minerals licensing remain under discussion via the Board of Trade. No major new tariff escalations reported; broader permanent resolution or further extension remains open, with Bessent noting incomplete Chinese agricultural commitments. Bilateral trade volumes remain well below 2022 peaks.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The yen trades near 157.5–158 per dollar after the Bank of Japan held its policy rate at 1.25% on October 30 (8-1 vote). The BOJ struck a hawkish tone, upgraded inflation projections (core ~2% consistent with target), accelerated ETF sales, and left the door open for a December hike. Markets had already priced a hold. Japan has spent ~¥27 trillion on yen-buying interventions in 2026 (April–May and July–August rounds, including a rare joint U.S. operation), with 160 treated as a practical red line. The rate differential versus the Fed (3.75–4%) continues to weigh on the yen; verbal warnings from Japanese officials remain active. Broader central-bank trend: Fed, ECB, and RBNZ all held rates in late October amid elevated inflation and geopolitical uncertainty.
